points.en: An illustration is a story or image inside the sermon that throws light on a point already stated, a window in the wall of the sermon (Spurgeon).
It serves a point within a larger structure, usually a deductive sermon, whereas in the story sermon the story is the whole message and carries all the weight.
Illustrations are all around a watchful preacher (Scripture, history, nature, news, literature, daily life), but what is noticed and not captured is lost, so he needs a file or system.
The accumulated file is the treasury the controlling-story sermon draws on, since that form rewards a preacher who has gathered good, truthful stories over years.
Names several of the ten types, such as personal experience, biblical, historical, biographical, nature, current event, quotation, hypothetical, analogy, humor.
Discusses the strength and caution of two types, e.g. personal experience is intimate and powerful but risks self-display; current events are vivid but spoil quickly.
It is dishonest to tell another's story as one's own; the clothesline preacher hangs out other men's washing as if it were his, which is pulpit plagiarism.
The remedy is honest attribution, such as I read of a man who... or a friend told me, which costs little and keeps integrity and trust.
The unit's two examples (the goat story and the George Street story) are told openly as borrowed and lose no power, showing attribution in practice.
A true story must stay true: it may be told vividly but not improved into something that did not happen.
A hypothetical must be signaled as suppose and a legend must not be passed off as fact.
This parallels Unit 4's rule not to add to the text: truth in the illustration as in the passage.
Get permission from real people, such as a congregant or family member, and guard their privacy and dignity, changing what should be changed.
Never use the pulpit to expose or embarrass someone who cannot answer back, because the story must not wound the people the truth is meant to save.
An illustration serves the point and the exposition; it is a window, not the building, and a wall that is all windows cannot stand.
When ignored, the sermon becomes a string of anecdotes with little Scripture, and the hearers remember the story but not the point, so the window has become the view.
Counsel him that presenting borrowed stories as his own experience is dishonest, pulpit plagiarism that undermines his integrity and the trust of his people.
Advise him to keep using the stories but credit them honestly, for example I read of a man who..., so truthful telling matches the truth he preaches.
Humor can open a closed heart or face and rest the hearer, so it serves a sermon as an illustration.
Its line: it must serve the truth, never mock the sacred, never wound a person present, and never grow until it becomes the point of the sermon.
The answer states a doctrinal point and proposes a specific illustration that genuinely fits and serves that point.
It names the type of the illustration (e.g. personal, biblical, historical, hypothetical) and its source.
It shows honest handling: credit to the source if borrowed, or the signal suppose if hypothetical, and the story told truthfully.
